reason: The sources provide more than 15 verified claims across multiple independent sites detailing the mission costs, specific unit mismatch, and investigation results.
story: In 1999, NASA lost a $125 million spacecraft due to a simple conversion error. The Mars Climate Orbiter was a 'Faster, Better, Cheaper' era probe designed to study the Martian climate. After a nine-month journey, it prepared for orbital insertion, but instead of entering its intended orbit, it disappeared. An investigation revealed a critical mismatch: the builder, Lockheed Martin, used imperial units (pound-force) for thruster data, while NASA’s navigation team expected metric units (newtons). A pound-force is 4.45 times stronger than a newton; this error pushed the probe to an altitude of only 57 kilometers—far below the 80-kilometer survival limit. The orbiter was either incinerated in the atmosphere or skipped off into deep space. Navigators had flagged the trajectory discrepancy before arrival, but their concerns were dismissed due to procedural rules, resulting in one of NASA's most expensive math mistakes.
angle: A $125 million NASA spacecraft was lost because engineers forgot to convert pounds to newtons, causing it to crash into Mars instead of orbiting it.

claims.claim: The Mars Climate Orbiter was launched on December 11, 1998.
Communication with the spacecraft was permanently lost on September 23, 1999.
The spacecraft was built by Lockheed Martin.
The mission was managed by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL).
The orbiter spacecraft alone cost approximately $125 million.
The failure was caused by one team using English/Imperial units and another using SI/Metric units.
Lockheed Martin's software provided impulse data in pound-force seconds.
NASA's navigation software expected data in newton-seconds.
One pound-force is equal to 4.45 newtons.
The mission was part of NASA’s 'Faster, Better, Cheaper' initiative.
The Mars Surveyor '98 program was estimated to be underfunded by at least 30%.
The actual altitude reached during insertion was approximately 57 kilometers (35 miles).
The minimum survival altitude for the orbiter was estimated at 80 kilometers (50 miles).
The spacecraft journey to Mars took approximately nine months.
The probe was likely either destroyed in the atmosphere or skipped off into heliocentric space.
The error was located in software used for modeling trajectory from 'Small Forces' thruster firings.
The spacecraft team was located in Colorado while the navigation team was in California.

disputed: The total project cost is listed as $327.6 million in Wikipedia [S1] but $285 million in PBS [S3]; the script should use the $327 million figure for the full program or $125 million for the orbiter.
The targeted insertion altitude is cited as 226 km in [S1] but 85 to 95 miles (approx 140 km) in [S6]; the script should describe the intended orbit as significantly higher than 100 kilometers.

Whether the error was detected: [S1] reports two navigators noticed concerns that were dismissed, while [S4] states no one detected the error; the script should attribute the ignored warnings to the investigation report findings.
